summary: India's folk dances are community dances tied to harvests, seasons, festivals, weddings and work. Well-known examples by state include Bhangra and Giddha (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Ghoomar (Rajasthan), Lavani (Maharashtra), Bihu (Assam), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Chhau (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal) and Cheraw (Mizoram).

paras: A folk dance belongs to a community rather than to a trained elite. It is learned by watching and joining in, performed at harvests, weddings, fairs and festivals, and changes from village to village. Unlike the [classical dances of India](classical-dances-of-india.html), folk dances usually have no written grammar and no single authority deciding the correct form.

Many are linked to the farming year: sowing, monsoon and harvest. Others belong to particular occupations, such as fishing communities, or to rites of passage. Tribal dances form a large and distinct group, often performed in a circle or line with drums, and closely linked to clan and village life. Our guide to [tribes of India](tribes-of-india.html) gives more of that background.

sections.h2: Famous folk dances of India, explained
paras: Bhangra began as a harvest dance of Punjabi farmers, performed to the dhol after the wheat harvest. Its energy and big arm movements made it a global form, especially in the diaspora. Giddha is the women's counterpart, built around clapping and short sung verses called boliyan.

Garba is danced in circles during the nine nights of Navratri, traditionally around a lamp in a pot. The circle form is very old in western India, and Garba's inscription on UNESCO's intangible list in 2023 recognised it as living heritage shared across communities.

Bihu is the dance of Assam's spring festival, Rongali Bihu, performed by young men and women with the dhol, pepa (buffalo-horn pipe) and taka. Chhau is a martial dance found in three styles: Purulia and Seraikela use masks, Mayurbhanj does not. Its moves echo combat training, a link explored in our lecture on [martial arts and society](martial-arts-and-society.html).

sections.h2: Why folk dances matter as heritage
paras: Folk dances carry information that books rarely record: songs in local dialects, farming calendars, clan histories, ideas about gender and community. They are a core part of India's [intangible cultural heritage](what-is-intangible-cultural-heritage.html), and several, including Kalbelia, Chhau and Garba, are on UNESCO's list.

They are also vulnerable. Migration, film music and stage versions can replace local variety with one standard form. Recording elders, learning songs with their words, and noting where and when a dance is performed are simple ways to keep the knowledge, as taught in our [oral history and neighbourhood memory lab](oral-history-and-neighbourhood-memory-lab.html).

sections.h2: Folk dances of India: notes for students
list: Folk dances are community-based and usually tied to harvest, season, festival or ritual.
Punjab: Bhangra and Giddha. Gujarat: Garba and Dandiya. Rajasthan: Ghoomar and Kalbelia.
Assam: Bihu. Mizoram: Cheraw (bamboo dance). Maharashtra: Lavani.
Chhau has three styles: Purulia, Seraikela and Mayurbhanj.
UNESCO-listed folk forms include Kalbelia, Chhau and Garba.
Yakshagana (Karnataka) and Theyyam (Kerala) are ritual or theatrical forms often grouped with folk dance.

faq.q: Which folk dance belongs to which state?
faq.a: Some well-known pairs: Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Ghoomar (Rajasthan), Lavani (Maharashtra), Bihu (Assam), Cheraw (Mizoram), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Theyyam (Kerala), Karagattam (Tamil Nadu), Nati (Himachal Pradesh) and Rouf (Jammu and Kashmir).

faq.q: What is the difference between folk and classical dance?
faq.a: Classical dances have a codified grammar, long training and a theoretical base in texts like the Natya Shastra. Folk dances belong to communities, are learned by joining in, change from place to place and are tied to festivals, harvests and life events.

faq.q: Which Indian folk dances are on the UNESCO list?
faq.a: Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan, Chhau dance of eastern India and the Garba of Gujarat are on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Manipur's Sankirtana, which includes dance, is also listed.

faq.q: Which state is the bamboo dance from?
faq.a: The best-known bamboo dance is Cheraw from Mizoram, in which dancers step in and out of pairs of bamboo poles clapped together in rhythm. Similar bamboo dances are found elsewhere in northeast and southeast Asia.

faq.q: Is Chhau a folk or classical dance?
faq.a: Chhau is generally classed as a folk or tribal martial dance. It is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, and the Ministry of Culture has at times included it among classical forms, but the Sangeet Natak Akademi's list of eight does not include it.

posts.caption: Purulia and Seraikela dancers wear masks. Mayurbhanj dancers do not. All three draw on combat moves, and Chhau is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

posts.hook: Ask about the songs, not just the steps.
posts.caption: Folk dances carry words: farming calendars, jokes, family histories. Record the lyrics with their meaning next time you see one performed.
